items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This paper presents the first K‐feldspar post‐infrared infrared (pIRIR) dating of river terrace deposits from the Avon valley, a major northern tributary of the palaeo‐Solent. Five pIRIR samples were obtained from three altitudinally distinct terraces (T10, T7 and T5), all previously dated using quartz OSL. While earlier OSL ages plateaued at ~300–350 ka, K‐feldspar pIRIR
                    <jats:sub>250</jats:sub>
                     age estimates extend terrace chronologies beyond this limit, yielding minimum ages of 535 ± 81 ka (T10), 429 ± 55 ka (T7) and 255 ± 33 ka and 245 ± 28 ka (T5). The pIRIR ages increase systematically with terrace altitude, diverge from quartz OSL results for the higher, older terraces, and are more consistent with expected stratigraphic relationships than the OSL dates. Integration of these ages with valley morphostratigraphy links terrace formation in the Avon valley to 100 ka glacial–interglacial cycles and places the archaeologically important Woodgreen site (T7) no later than MIS 11−10. The revised chrono‐geomorphological framework allows improved correlation of Avon terraces with sequences across the Solent region, promotes the use of paired OSL‐pIRIR dating to elucidate localised maximum age limits for OSL and increase the reliability of mid‐Pleistocene age estimates, and provides new age constraints for Pleistocene landscape evolution and hominin activity at the north‐western margin of Europe.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Upper Triassic turbidites of the Tethyan Himalaya record an abrupt influx of 300−200 Ma detrital zircons, contrasting with underlying and overlying successions. Although the Terra Australis orogen provenance of these zircons has been widely discussed, the controls on this influx during the Carnian remain unresolved. We combine new zircon U-Pb results from five Songre Formation tuffaceous siltstones with published biostratigraphy and compiled detrital zircon U-Pb-Hf isotopic data. Maximum depositional ages and fossils support Carnian deposition, overlapping within uncertainty with the Carnian Pluvial Episode (CPE, ca. 234−232 Ma). Detrital zircons of 300−200 Ma yield εHf(t) values from −13.1 to +14.9, compatible with mixed input from multiple Terra Australis orogen sectors, including Antarctic sources. We infer that CPE-related hydrological intensification likely enhanced erosion and sediment evacuation from an already active high-latitude orogen, producing a distal signal in the Tethyan Himalaya. The results highlight how transient climate perturbations can amplify sediment routing from active orogenic source regions without requiring a unique tectonic trigger.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Naked mole‐rats (
                    <jats:italic>Heterocephalus glaber</jats:italic>
                    ) are eusocial rodents with unusually long lifespans. Adaptations to their subterranean habitat include large, well‐innervated incisors used for digging underground tunnel systems; oral folds that close behind the incisors; and a specialized tactile system (sensitive incisors in addition to tactile hairs that cover the entire body). This well‐developed tactile system compensates for their reduced visual and auditory systems. Naked mole‐rats are functionally blind and have small eyes, even compared to other African mole‐rat species. They also have relatively poor auditory capabilities as well as absent pinnae. Although few studies have characterized the facial musculature of naked mole‐rats, their facial musculature would be expected to have evolved commensurately with adaptations to a subterranean niche. To examine this, we performed detailed dissections of superficial facial musculature in adult naked mole‐rats. This included muscle identification and characterization of attachment sites compared to what has previously been shown in rats. Our dissections demonstrated reduced musculature associated with the eyes (e.g., orbicularis oculi), the ears (e.g., auricularis posterior and interscutularis muscles), and the dorsal head (frontalis and occipitalis muscles), but well‐developed musculature facilitating movements of the nose and mouth, befitting the roles of these anatomical structures in sensory perception and social interactions. Our findings not only provide insights into the evolutionary adaptations of naked mole‐rat facial musculature to a subterranean niche, but will also help inform future studies assessing and interpreting social‐emotional communication in naked mole‐rats through the lens of species‐specific adaptations in the musculature underlying facial expressions.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Mikaela D. Thurber, Diana K. Sarko
